html:
The Yayoi period is the age in Japan when wet-rice farming, bronze and iron arrived from the Asian mainland, between the end of the Jōmon period and the rise of great burial mounds around 250 CE. Its start is debated: the old date is about 300 BCE, while newer dating puts the first rice paddies in northern Kyushu as early as the 10th to 8th century BCE.

The change came with migrants from the Korean peninsula, who brought paddy fields, new tools and new pottery. They mixed with the Jōmon foragers already there. Farming spread east through the islands over several centuries, though not to Hokkaido.

What the Yayoi period brought:

  • Rice farming in irrigated paddies, which fed a much larger population.
  • Bronze and iron. Bronze was mostly for ritual objects, like the bell-shaped dōtaku, mirrors and blades; iron was for tools and weapons.
  • Simpler, more useful pottery, named after the Yayoi district of Tokyo where it was first found in 1884.
  • Moated and walled villages, like Yoshinogari in Kyushu, and signs of war.

By the 1st century CE many small chiefdoms had formed, which Chinese histories called the land of Wa. The Records of the Three Kingdoms, a Chinese history, tells of a queen named Himiko who ruled many of these chiefdoms in the 3rd century and sent envoys to China.

From around 250 CE great keyhole-shaped tombs were built, marking the start of the Kofun period and the rise of the Yamato state.
